holidays.name: No News is Good News Day
holidays.description: A day to take a break from the doom-scrolling and headlines, and to enjoy some peace and quiet from the constant news cycle. Turn off the TV, mute the push alerts, and bask in blissful ignorance.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance that grew from the old proverb 'no news is good news,' which dates back to at least the 1600s. King James I of England is often credited with an early version of the saying.
holidays.funFact: The proverb 'no news is good news' was used in a 1616 letter by King James I, who wrote that 'no news is better than evil news.'

holidays.name: Make Your Bed Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to the humble act of pulling up the sheets and fluffing the pillows. Fans say it starts your day with a small win, while rebels enjoy a guilt-free tangle of blankets.
holidays.origin: An informal, modern observance promoted by home and lifestyle brands, popularized by the idea that making your bed is the first accomplished task of the day.
holidays.funFact: A 2017 survey by a mattress company found that bed makers were more likely to report liking their jobs and feeling well rested, though experts note that correlation isn't causation.

holidays.name: Hot Cross Bun Day (Hot Cross Bun Observance)
holidays.description: A day to enjoy spiced, fruit-studded buns marked with a sweet cross on top, usually eaten around Easter but celebrated by dedicated bakers and carb enthusiasts off-season.
holidays.origin: Hot cross buns have been eaten in England for centuries, traditionally on Good Friday. A nursery rhyme about them dates to the 1700s, and the buns became a symbol of Easter observance.
holidays.funFact: Superstition held that a hot cross bun baked on Good Friday would never go moldy, and some English households hung one from the kitchen rafters for a whole year as a good luck charm.

holidays.name: Patriot Day and National Day of Service and Remembrance
holidays.description: Not a quirky party day, but a solemn observance in the United States honoring the victims of the September 11, 2001 attacks. Many people mark it with moments of silence, memorial events, and volunteering.
holidays.origin: Patriot Day was established by a joint resolution of Congress in 2001, and the National Day of Service and Remembrance was added in 2009 to encourage charitable acts in honor of those lost.
holidays.funFact: The flag is flown at half-staff on Patriot Day, and the 9/11 Day of Service has become one of the largest annual volunteer efforts in the United States, encouraging acts of kindness and community service.
